extracted.intended_audience: readers of entertainment news / followers of comedy and media controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and evaluating a comedian's past social-media jokes and the ensuing public backlash; the page collects offending tweets, public reactions, and defenses to illustrate why a hire is controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-Semitic and sexist content in jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets being labeled as anti-Semitic and sexist (the article lists example tweets such as 'Messi... just like jewish chicks', 'Almost bumped a Jewish kid...', 'Behind every successful Rap Billionaire is a double as rich Jewish man', and several jokes targeting women, fat people, and lesbians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are presented as crossing a line from 'jokes' into hate/offensive territory; public critics labeled the tweets anti-Semitic and sexist and used them to question the suitability of the hire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to clean up social-media history before a high-profile hire
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics noted old tweets were uncovered quickly after the announcement; commentary includes 'Weird that Trevor Noah didn’t do a quick twitter cleanup before getting the job.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied best practice: review and remove or address problematic past posts prior to major public appointments to reduce predictable backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer vetting and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Several reactions target Comedy Central's hiring decision (e.g., 'your new hire @Trevornoah = racist Jew hater' and 'nobody at Comedy Central knows how to do a Twitter search').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations are judged on their vetting processes; failure to check public social-media history can reflect poorly on the employer and fuel criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and identity affect judgments of offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some defenders argued context/identity matter—e.g., 'People digging up old tweets... He’s racist?? Uhmm a multi-racial comedian is racist??'—raising the point that a comedian's background influences how remarks are interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of whether material is racist or sexist may vary depending on the comedian's identity, intent, and broader context; defenders used this to push back against accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic quality and writing support as a mitigating factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics suggested the jokes themselves show poor quality or lack of refinement (comments include 'My biggest takeaway... is that he’s in desperate need of a good writing staff').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-quality or lazy jokes are more likely to be criticized and less defensible as 'edgy' comedy; having strong writers can reduce reliance on crude stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived double standards in tolerance for offensive jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers noted inconsistent treatment of offensive material depending on who makes it (example: 'Interesting that white comics make offensive jokes and are celebrated or tolerated but Trevor Noah well that’s not acceptable.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reaction may be shaped by perceived double standards, which becomes part of the controversy narrative and affects reputational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity amplification and public callouts escalate controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: The article compiles many celebrity and public tweets calling him anti-Semitic, racist, or sexist (e.g., Roseanne Barr, David Draiman, Dani Klein), demonstrating how influential voices amplify incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When high-profile figures publicly condemn someone, the controversy spreads rapidly and increases pressure on both the comedian and their employer; monitoring likely amplifiers is important.
